title: Black Government Conference & RNA Founding
body:
The Republic of New Afrika was founded in March 1968 at the Black Government Conference in Detroit, convened by the brothers Milton and Richard Henry — who took the names Gaidi and Imari Obadele — along with some 500 Black nationalists. Drawing on the legacy of Malcolm X, the conference proclaimed the creation of an independent Black nation and adopted a founding document, the New Afrikan Declaration of Independence.

The RNA demanded three things: an independent Black-majority nation carved from the five Deep South states of Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama, Georgia, and South Carolina; billions of dollars in reparations for slavery; and a plebiscite allowing Black Americans to choose their citizenship. It framed Black Americans as a colonized, captive nation entitled to self-determination under international law.

title: Declaration of Independence & Provisional Government
body:
At its 1968 founding the Republic of New Afrika issued a Declaration of Independence and established a Provisional Government of the Republic of New Afrika (PGRNA), complete with officers, a legislature, and a president — the exiled author of Negroes with Guns, Robert F. Williams, chosen in absentia, with the Obadele brothers in leading roles.

The provisional-government framework was central to the RNA's strategy: by declaring an existing government of an already-independent nation, the organization asserted that Black Americans were not seeking rights within the United States but exercising sovereignty over their own captured nation. This national-liberation posture shaped everything that followed, including its confrontations with U.S. law enforcement.

title: New Bethel Incident
body:
On March 29, 1969, the RNA held its first-anniversary conference at the New Bethel Baptist Church in Detroit — the church of Reverend C.L. Franklin, father of Aretha Franklin. As the meeting ended, a confrontation outside left one police officer dead and another wounded. Police then fired on and stormed the church, arresting nearly 150 people inside.

In the aftermath, Judge George Crockett Jr., a Black jurist, convened an emergency court and released most of those held without charge, condemning the mass arrest as a violation of their constitutional rights — a stand that made him a target of white political fury. The New Bethel Incident became an early flashpoint in the RNA's history and a landmark in Detroit's long conflict between the Black community and the police.

title: New Bethel Acquittals
body:
In the trials that followed the New Bethel Incident, the RNA members charged in the shooting were ultimately acquitted. Clarence Fuller and Alfred 2X Hibbitt were tried for the killing of the officer, and the juries declined to convict.

The acquittals were a significant setback for the authorities and a vindication for the RNA, which argued that its members had acted in self-defense against a police assault. But the episode also marked the RNA as a target for sustained surveillance and repression by both local police and the FBI.

title: Relocation toward Mississippi Organizing
body:
In the late 1960s and early 1970s the RNA shifted its focus toward the Deep South, and especially Mississippi, which it claimed as the territorial heart of the proposed nation of New Afrika. The organization sought to purchase land, build settlements, and organize among rural Black Southerners, attempting to give concrete form to its claim of national sovereignty.

In 1971 the provisional government relocated its capital to Mississippi and acquired farmland near Jackson for a projected capital city, "El Malik." This move into the Deep South — the region where the RNA claimed a nation — brought it into direct collision with Mississippi authorities and the FBI.

title: Jackson, Mississippi Shootout
body:
On August 18, 1971, a combined force of Jackson police and FBI agents raided two RNA houses in Jackson, Mississippi, at dawn, using an armored vehicle and heavy weapons. A gun battle erupted; Jackson police officer William Skinner was killed and two other officers were wounded.

Eleven RNA members were arrested and charged. The raid, part of the FBI's broader campaign against Black nationalist organizations, effectively crushed the RNA's Mississippi project and initiated the prosecutions that would imprison much of its leadership.

title: RNA-11 Prosecutions
body:
The eleven RNA members arrested after the August 1971 Jackson raid — known as the RNA-11 — faced long and grueling prosecutions in state and federal court on charges including murder, treason against the state of Mississippi, and assault. Several were convicted and given lengthy sentences.

The RNA-11 argued that they were prisoners of a national-liberation war and victims of a coordinated government attack, and their cases became a rallying point for the Black liberation movement. The prosecutions, and the decades some members spent in prison, made the RNA-11 enduring figures in the U.S. political-prisoner tradition.

title: Imari Obadele’s Imprisonment
body:
Imari Abubakari Obadele (born Richard Henry), co-founder and president of the Provisional Government of the Republic of New Afrika, was among those imprisoned after the 1971 Jackson raid, convicted on federal charges arising from the shootout. He served years in federal prison, becoming one of the most prominent New Afrikan political prisoners.

After his release Obadele earned a doctorate and became a scholar and organizer, co-founding the National Coalition of Blacks for Reparations in America (N'COBRA) and continuing to press the RNA's demands for independence and reparations. His imprisonment and later career linked the RNA's 1970s struggle to the enduring reparations movement.

title: The Continuing New Afrikan Prisoner Tradition
body:
The Republic of New Afrika's politics of New Afrikan national self-determination profoundly influenced later Black liberation organizations and the broader political-prisoner movement. Its framework — that Black Americans constitute a captive New Afrikan nation with the right to independence — was adopted by activists across the Black liberation underground, and many later prisoners identified as New Afrikan citizens.

Figures shaped by or aligned with RNA politics — among them members of the Black Liberation Army and long-held prisoners such as Mutulu Shakur and Russell Maroon Shoatz — carried the New Afrikan tradition into the decades of political-prisoner organizing that followed. The RNA's insistence on self-determination and reparations remains an influence on Black radical thought today.
